666.title: Hanukkah: the oil (Shabbat 21b)
666.hook: the Talmud's story of one jar of oil lasting eight days
666.howItsDone: Many Jews light Hanukkah lamps with olive oil to recall the jar in the Talmud's story, and eat foods fried in oil, like latkes and sufganiyot, during the eight nights.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maccabees, and a new altar dedicated for eight days. Your line was the few against the many. Today, the same eight days, told a very different way.

One little jar of oil, enough for one night, and it burned for eight. That's the Hanukkah of greeting cards and children's books, and it's why people eat foods fried in oil. But yesterday's story, from First Maccabees, doesn't mention oil at all. The jar comes from a page of the Talmud, in the middle of a long discussion about which wicks and oils you may use for Shabbat candles. And it starts with a question that sounds almost naive.
screen: `ONE JAR, EIGHT NIGHTS.` → `FIRST MACCABEES DOESN'T SAY IT.` → `ONE PAGE OF THE TALMUD.`

segments.voice: The question, in tractate Shabbat, page 21b, is simply: what is Hanukkah? As if the rabbis are asking why keep it at all. The answer is a short story. When the Greeks entered the Temple, they made all the oils impure. When the Hasmonean family, the Maccabees, defeated them, they searched and found just one jar of oil still sealed with the high priest's seal. It held enough to light the lamp for a single day. A miracle happened, and they lit from it for eight days. The next year, the story ends, they set those days as festival days, for praise and thanksgiving. That's the whole account: a few lines. Notice what it leaves out. No battles, no Judah, no Antiochus. Readers explain this differently. Some suggest that after later revolts against Rome ended in disaster, the rabbis preferred to stress God's quiet help over victory in battle. Others point out that the Talmud seems to assume its readers know the history, and only adds what's missing. Either way, the story on the greeting cards is this one: not a war, but a lamp. And its point is small and stubborn. A sealed jar, one day's worth, nowhere near enough. They lit it anyway. That's the miracle the rabbis chose to remember: not that there was plenty, but that the little they had was enough to begin.
screen: `WHAT IS HANUKKAH?` · `ONE JAR, THE HIGH PRIEST'S SEAL.` · `ONE DAY'S OIL, EIGHT DAYS' LIGHT.` · `A LAMP, NOT A WAR.` · then, large: `A LITTLE LASTS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you have only a little of right now: time, patience, energy, hope. Instead of waiting until there's enough, picture spending that little on purpose, like one kind word with the patience you have left. Breathe slowly, as if you're watching a small flame hold.
Hanukkah. The dedication, and in the Talmud's telling, the eight days one jar of oil kept burning. Today's word.
Your line: a little lasts. The jar was never enough, and they lit it anyway. See you tomorrow.

667.title: Hanukkah: show the light
667.hook: the lights go where passers-by can see
667.howItsDone: Families light the Hanukkah menorah at nightfall, adding one light each night, and place it by the door or in a window facing the street so passers-by can see; many communities also hold public menorah lightings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hanukkah's jar of oil, one day's worth, burning for eight. Your line was a little lasts. Today, where the light goes once it's lit.

An early winter evening, a street of houses and apartments. In one window, a row of small flames. In another, a little glass box by the front door, with oil lamps inside. On an apartment balcony, electric bulbs. Plenty of what happens in a Jewish home stays inside, among family. These lights are different. They're placed so that someone walking past, who may not know or care what they mean, can see them. And there's a rule behind that, with a two-word name.
screen: `FLAMES IN THE WINDOWS.` → `A GLASS BOX BY THE DOOR.` → `FOR SOMEONE WALKING PAST.`

segments.voice: Pirsumei nisa is Aramaic. It means publicizing the miracle, and it sits behind many of the rules about where and when the Hanukkah lights are lit. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says the lamp should be set at the entrance of the house, on the outside. If you live upstairs, you place it in a window facing the public street. Its time is from when the sun goes down until the last people have gone home from the market, because that's when the street is full of people to see it. You may not even use the Hanukkah light for anything practical, like reading. That's one reason for the extra candle, the shammash, the helper: you use that one, and the others are just for showing. Then comes a striking line. In a time of danger, the Talmud says, it's enough to set the lamp on your table inside. Showing the light matters, but not more than a life. Families in dangerous times and places have done exactly that, lighting quietly, indoors. In safer times and places the lights came back out to the windows, and in some cities to giant public lamps in town squares. The principle is the same in every case: a miracle that stays private isn't finished being told. The lights are meant to be noticed, and the person who notices doesn't have to be Jewish, or even curious. They just have to walk by.

segments.voice: Look back over the last week and find one good thing: a kindness someone did for you, a worry that turned out fine, a small win. Picture who might like to hear it. Then sit with the good thing itself, quietly, like a flame in a window.

668.title: Hanukkah: Maoz Tzur
668.hook: a medieval song sung after lighting, recalling many rescues
668.howItsDone: In many Ashkenazi homes, the family sings Maoz Tzur together after lighting the Hanukkah candles each night, usually the first verse; Sephardi and Mizrahi families often sing other hymns or Psalm 30.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pirsumei nisa, the lights placed where passers-by can see. Your line was show the light. Today, what people sing once the lights are lit.

The candles are lit. The blessings are said. Kids are already eyeing the doughnuts. Then, in many homes, before anyone moves, someone starts a song. Plenty of people know the tune but not most of the words; they hum through the middle and come back loud for the end. Many families sing only the first verse. But it has six, and if you read them all, it isn't only a song about Hanukkah. It's a song about a lot of nights like this one.
screen: `THE CANDLES ARE LIT.` → `PLENTY KNOW THE TUNE.` → `SIX VERSES, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: The song is called Maoz Tzur. Maoz means stronghold, a fortress. Tzur means rock. The Torah uses rock as a name for God; in the old Jewish translation, Moses sings, "The Rock, His work is perfect." So the song opens by calling God the fortress-rock of my salvation. Who wrote it? The poet signed it the way medieval Hebrew poets liked: the first letters of the first five verses spell a name, Mordechai. Nobody knows for certain who this Mordechai was. Now the verses. The first looks forward to a rebuilt Temple. The second remembers slavery in Egypt, and the way out. The third, the exile to Babylon, and the return after seventy years. The fourth, Haman, who wanted to destroy the Jews of Persia, in the story Purim tells. Only the fifth gets to the Greeks, the Hasmoneans and the jar of oil. And the sixth, likely added later, asks for one more rescue, in the poet's own time. So Hanukkah, in this song, is one link in a chain. Danger, then rescue. Danger, then rescue. People sang it in places where the danger was not ancient history. The English version some families sing, Rock of Ages, is a loose adaptation rather than a translation. And Sephardi and Mizrahi families often sing other songs, or other tunes. The words that travel everywhere are the first two: fortress, rock.

669.title: The Tenth of Tevet
669.hook: a fast for the siege of Jerusalem, now also a day of Kaddish for those whose death date is unknown
669.tomorrow: Tu BiShvat: a seder of fruits
669.howItsDone: On the Tenth of Tevet, observant Jews fast from dawn until nightfall and add Selichot prayers; in many communities, especially in Israel, Kaddish is said and candles lit for Holocaust victims whose date of death is unknown.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maoz Tzur, the song of many rescues. Your line was rock of ages. Today, a short winter fast, for a time the rescue didn't come.

Many Jewish families keep a yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death. A candle burns for a day, a son or daughter says Kaddish in the synagogue, someone tells a story at dinner. It's a date that holds a life. But what if you don't have the date? What if a whole branch of your family tree simply stops, in a town that no longer exists, in a year you can only guess, and nobody survived to say which day? For millions of Jewish families after the Holocaust, that was not a hypothetical. And the answer they were given was a fast day two and a half thousand years old.
screen: `A DATE THAT HOLDS A LIFE.` → `WHAT IF THERE IS NO DATE?` → `AN OLD FAST, A NEW TASK.`

segments.voice: The Tenth of Tevet remembers where the destruction of Jerusalem began. The book of Kings gives the date. In the old Jewish translation: "in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month," Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against Jerusalem with his whole army and laid siege to it. That siege ended about a year and a half later, with the city broken and the Temple burned. The prophet Zechariah already names the fasts that grew up around these losses, among them "the fast of the tenth," and adds a promise: they will one day become times of joy and gladness. People fast from dawn until nightfall and add special prayers of repentance. It's one of the shorter fasts; the night before is not included, and anyone ill, pregnant or nursing is usually excused. Health comes first. Then, in the years after the Holocaust, Israel's Chief Rabbinate gave the day a second purpose. It became the general day of Kaddish: a day for saying the mourner's prayer for those whose date of death is unknown. Many of the six million have no known yahrzeit. On the Tenth of Tevet, their children and grandchildren, and people with no known connection to them at all, say Kaddish for them and light candles. Holocaust Remembrance Day, in the spring, is the date most people know. But for many communities this older fast carries the same names: a siege that began the losses, and a day that gives a date to the dead who never got one.
screen: `THE TENTH MONTH, THE TENTH DAY.` · `THE SIEGE OF JERUSALEM BEGINS.` · `ZECHARIAH: THE FAST OF THE TENTH.` · `A KADDISH FOR UNKNOWN DATES.` · then, large: `FOR THE UNKNOWN DATES.`

Hold the fact that they lived, and that they were someone's child. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer; if not, simply sit with them in silence.

670.title: Tu BiShvat: a seder of fruits
670.hook: the Safed mystics made a seder of fruits and four cups of wine
670.howItsDone: Many Jews eat fruits of the Land of Israel on Tu BiShvat, especially the seven species, and some hold a Tu BiShvat seder following the kabbalists' order of fruits and four cups of wine moving from white to red.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tenth of Tevet's general day of Kaddish. Your line was for the unknown dates. Today, a month later, the trees.

It begins as a line in a tax code. The Mishnah lists four new years in the Jewish calendar, and one is for trees. Why do trees need a new year? Because the Torah's tithes and fruit laws count a tree's age, and someone has to decide when its year turns over. The schools of Shammai and Hillel disagreed about the date, and Hillel's view won: the fifteenth of the month of Shevat. In Hebrew numbers, fifteen is written tet-vav, said tu. Tu BiShvat. For a long time, it was mostly a date for bookkeeping. Then a group of mystics sat down at a table and turned it into a feast.
screen: `FOUR NEW YEARS.` → `ONE IS FOR TREES.` → `FROM BOOKKEEPING TO A FEAST.`

segments.voice: The mystics were kabbalists in the tradition of Safed, the hill town in the Galilee where a circle of Jewish mystics gathered. Their followers wrote a little book, later printed as Pri Etz Hadar, fruit of the goodly tree. It lays out a Tu BiShvat seder, an ordered meal like Passover's, but made of fruit. First, the fruits of the Land of Israel. The Torah praises the land, in the old Jewish translation, as "a land of wheat and barley, and vines and fig-trees and pomegranates; a land of olive-trees and honey." The rabbis read that honey as date honey. Seven species, and the seder makes sure to eat them. Then the fruits are sorted into three groups: a hard shell outside, like walnuts and pomegranates; a hard pit inside, like olives and dates; and ones you can eat completely, like figs and grapes. For the mystics, these stood for layers of the world, from the most guarded to the most open. Then four cups of wine: white, then white with a little red, then mostly red, then all red. Some read it as winter warming into spring. A blessing is said over each new fruit, with passages from the Bible and the Zohar read between. Today families, schools and environmental groups hold Tu BiShvat seders, some traditional, some new. At the heart of the old order is a simple act: paying attention to what grows on a tree, and saying a blessing before eating it.
screen: `THE MYSTICS OF SAFED.` · `THE SEVEN SPECIES.` · `SHELL, PIT, OR OPEN.` · `FOUR CUPS, WHITE TO RED.` · then, large: `FRUITS OF THE TREE.`

segments.voice: If you have fruit nearby, set out up to three kinds, one with a peel, one with a pit, one you can eat whole; if not, picture them. Look at one properly, its color, its weight, the tree it came from, and if you say blessings, this is a moment for one. Then eat slowly, noticing how each is different.
Tu BiShvat. The fifteenth of Shevat, the new year for trees, and for the mystics, a seder of fruits and four cups. Today's word.

671.title: Tu BiShvat: planting
671.hook: many plant trees or give to planting on this day
671.howItsDone: Many Jews plant trees on Tu BiShvat, especially in Israel, where schools hold planting days; elsewhere many give to tree-planting funds, eat fruits of the land, or care for plants at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mystics' Tu BiShvat seder, with its fruits and four cups. Your line was fruits of the tree. Today, the other half of the day: putting a tree in the ground.

A man walking along a road sees someone planting a carob tree. He stops and asks: how long until this tree bears fruit? Seventy years, comes the answer. The traveler looks him up and down. And you're sure you'll be alive in seventy years to eat from it? The planter keeps digging. That's a story from the Talmud, in tractate Taanit. The traveler is Choni, whom the same page remembers for praying down rain, and his story goes on to become something like Rip Van Winkle. But the planter's answer is the part people quote.
screen: `A MAN PLANTS A CAROB.` → `SEVENTY YEARS TO FRUIT.` → `WILL YOU BE ALIVE TO EAT IT?`

segments.voice: The planter says, roughly: I found this world full of carob trees. My ancestors planted them for me, so I'm planting for my children. Then Choni sits down to eat, falls asleep, and sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that very tree. Are you the one who planted it? No, the man says: my grandfather did. That's the Talmud's picture of planting: you do it for someone you may never meet. The midrash finds the same idea in the Torah's command to plant fruit trees when Israel enters the land. Even God, it notes, began the world by planting: Genesis says God planted a garden in Eden. So planting becomes a way of imitating God. Another teaching, in a collection called Avot of Rabbi Natan, is bolder still. It's attributed to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: if you're holding a sapling in your hand and someone tells you the Messiah has arrived, plant the sapling first. Then go out to greet him. Tu BiShvat became a planting day only in modern times. The story usually told is that a teacher in the village of Zikhron Yaakov took his students out to plant trees on the fifteenth of Shevat, and the custom spread through schools and, later, tree-planting campaigns. Today some people plant on this day, and others give money for planting. In the northern winter it's often too cold to dig, so people plant indoors, or give, or water what's already growing. Somebody planted for you.

segments.voice: If there's a plant near you, give it water now, slowly, and watch the soil drink; if not, picture a tree you've loved and whoever planted it. Then think of one person who planted something for you: a lesson, a habit, a kindness you're still eating from.
Tu BiShvat. The new year for trees, and in modern times, a day for planting what others will enjoy. Today's word.

672.title: The Fast of Esther (Esther 4:16)
672.hook: a fast the day before Purim, for Esther's three days of fasting
672.howItsDone: On the Fast of Esther, the thirteenth of Adar, observant Jews fast from dawn until nightfall, often give charity in the afternoon in memory of the half-shekel, and break the fast after hearing the Megillah read on Purim night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Choni's carob tree. Your line was plant something. Today, late winter, and the road to Purim.

A young woman is standing outside a door. Behind it sits the king of Persia, who also happens to be her husband. There's a law: anyone who walks into the king's inner court without being called is put to death, unless the king holds out his golden scepter. She hasn't been called in thirty days. And her people, the Jews of the Persian empire, have a date set for their destruction. Her cousin Mordecai has just told her that if she stays silent, she may not escape either. She doesn't go in yet. First, she sends back a message.
screen: `A DOOR SHE CAN'T WALK THROUGH.` → `NOT CALLED IN THIRTY DAYS.` → `FIRST, A MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Esther's message is in chapter four. She asks Mordecai to gather all the Jews of Shushan and fast for her: no food, no drink, for three days, night and day. She and her maids will fast too. Then she'll go in to the king, against the law. And her last words, in the old Jewish translation: "and if I perish, I perish." No speech about courage. Just a decision, and a fast to get ready for it. The Fast of Esther as people keep it today falls on the thirteenth of Adar, the day before Purim. But the book never dates Esther's own three-day fast, and its timeline leads tradition to place it in the spring month of Nisan, almost a year earlier. So why the thirteenth of Adar? That was the day set for the attack, the day the Jews had to defend themselves. Later authorities explain that people fasted and prayed on that day of battle, as they had with Esther. The book itself, near its end, mentions fasts and cries as part of what the Jews took on. The fast is first described as a custom after the Talmud's time, and it's one of the minor fasts: dawn to nightfall, and anyone ill, pregnant or nursing is usually excused. Health comes first. If Purim falls on a Sunday, the fast moves back to Thursday, so it doesn't land on Shabbat. In the afternoon there's a custom of giving coins to charity, recalling the half-shekel. And at nightfall the fast breaks straight into Purim: the scroll is read, and the feast begins. Hunger first. Then joy.
screen: `FAST FOR ME, THREE DAYS.` · `IF I PERISH, I PERISH.` · `WHY THE THIRTEENTH OF ADAR?` · `DAWN TO NIGHTFALL, THEN PURIM.` · then, large: `BEFORE THE FEAST, A FAST.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing to go without, a snack or a complaint you usually make, not to suffer but to get ready. Then think of one hard thing ahead, a conversation or a door you'll have to walk through, and let the small fast be your preparation.
Mordecai, Esther's cousin, who warned her that silence wouldn't save her, and whose message led to the fast before she risked her life before the king.
Your line: before the feast, a fast. From a little oil to a quiet decision. Until tomorrow.
